Posterior predictive checks on single-case visual-analysis features

Source: R/utils-ppc-features.R
posterior_predictive_features.Rd

Computes visual-analysis summary statistics on the observed data and on posterior-predictive replicate datasets, then returns the posterior predictive p-value for each statistic.

Usage

posterior_predictive_features(
  model,
  data = NULL,
  statistics = .ppc_statistics_all,
  n_draws = 500L,
  mode = c("same", "new"),
  ar_method = c("gls", "moment"),
  pool = c("case_means", "all_obs"),
  design = NULL
)

Arguments

model

A fitted brmsfit.

data

Data holding the outcome, case, phase and (optional) time columns; defaults to the model's data. Rows with a missing outcome are allowed: replicate values are set to NA there.

statistics

Character vector selecting which statistics to compute ("immediacy" selects all five time points).

n_draws

Number of posterior-predictive replicate datasets (default 500). The p-value is a proportion over these draws, so its Monte Carlo error is sqrt(p * (1 - p) / n_draws): about 0.007 at the 0.025 flag boundary with 500 draws and about 0.022 with 50, large enough at small n_draws that a value near the boundary can flag by chance.

mode

"same" replicates for the observed cases; "new" draws new case effects from the population posterior (allow_new_levels = TRUE) to assess generalization. In both modes an observation-level random effect (one level per fitted row) is redrawn rather than conditioned on, and replicate values are set to NA wherever the observed outcome is missing so both sides use the same rows.

ar_method

"gls" (default) or "moment" estimator for the autocorrelation statistic (see Details). "gls" needs the nlme package and falls back to "moment" with a message when it is not installed; it fits one model per replicate, so it is slower.

pool

"case_means" (default) or "all_obs": how the pooled level and absence rows combine tiers (see Details).

design

Design the model was fit with, as returned by detect_design_type. Only "alternating" changes the phase structure: conditions are pooled instead of being split into numbered runs. NULL (default) re-derives it from data, which can disagree with the design the model was fit with.

Value

A list with summary (one row per statistic/tier/phase, with columns statistic, case (the tier label, or "pooled"), phase (phase occurrence such as "B1"), observed, p_value, p_tie (share of replicates equal to the observed statistic), and flag; the pooled initial row is left out when it duplicates the pooled level row, see Details) and draws (long data frame of replicate values for density plots), and note (NULL, or how replicates were conditioned for an ar() model and which requested statistics were not computed and why). Empty data frames with a note if the case, phase, or outcome column is missing; an error if model is not a brmsfit or brms cannot produce posterior draws.

Details

Statistics are computed per tier (each combination of the grouping columns of tier_vars(), so a case identifier repeated across studies or a case measured on several behaviors gives separate series) and per phase occurrence within the tier: A1, B1, A2, B2, M1 (phase labels with a known role, see phase_role(), take the role letters; other labels keep their own). Each statistic is computed in each phase for each participant and pooled across participants. In an alternating-treatments design every session of a condition forms one phase.

  • initial: first baseline observation, compared with the replicate value at that session. When the model formula has no time term (a stable baseline level), every session of the initial baseline phase has the same predictive distribution, so each observation of that phase is compared with the replicate first session: the p-value averages the per-observation p-values and observed is the phase mean. The pooled row compares the mean of these tier phase means with the same mean computed on each replicate; under pool = "case_means" with level requested this equals the pooled level row of that baseline phase and is dropped. A variable in a fixed, random-effect, or smooth term counts as a time term when its name contains the time column name or starts with time, session, or trend (e.g. session_c). An ar(), ma(), or arma() term also counts, since its replicates condition on lagged residuals and so differ by session. The pooled initial row is an scdbayes addition; the published method defines initial performance per participant only.

  • level, trend, variability, absence: within-phase mean, OLS slope, SD, and proportion of outcomes \(\le 0\). Pooled rows average the tier means (level) and tier proportions (absence) with equal weight per tier under the default pool = "case_means", or use all observations of the phase under pool = "all_obs", as the published reference code does; the two differ only when tiers have unequal phase lengths. Trend pools the mean of the tier slopes and variability the within-tier pooled SD. Absence is computed for every family: for a continuous family it exposes a model that predicts values \(\le 0\) the data never show (for example a Normal model of a rate).

  • immediacy_t1 to immediacy_t5: time-specific treatment effects (TSTE) at each of the first five intervention time points, the observation minus the prediction of the regression line fitted to the preceding baseline phase, one row per adjacent baseline-to-intervention transition and a pooled mean per time point. Withdrawal transitions are not used.

  • nonoverlap: Tau between each pair of adjacent phases, the mean of the signs of all later-minus-earlier differences. Pairs are onsets (baseline to intervention, e.g. A1-B1, A2-B2) and, in reversal designs, withdrawals (intervention to baseline, e.g. B1-A2), reported as separate phase contrasts. The row's phase is the later phase of the pair, so "A2" is the B1-A2 withdrawal contrast.

  • autocorrelation: one Level-1 lag-1 estimate pooled across tiers. ar_method = "gls" (default) fits a generalized least squares model with nlme::gls() by REML: an intercept and a slope for each phase occurrence within tier (Case:Phase, A1, B1, A2, B2) with a common AR(1) correlation over sessions within tier, started at 0. For AB tiers this equals the binary phase indicator of Eq. A19; in reversal designs each phase keeps its own level, so level shifts between same-condition phases do not enter the residuals. ar_method = "moment" is a faster moment estimate from time-ordered residuals after each phase's level and trend are removed. The same estimator is applied to observed and replicate data.

The role of each phase (baseline vs intervention) only pairs phases for immediacy and non-overlap and colors the overlay plot. Immediacy and Tau are reported as later minus earlier on every row, whatever the intervention goal, so a decrease goal shows negative values. The extremeness flag is two-sided, so the orientation does not change which checks flag. The posterior predictive p-value is \(p = \Pr[T(y^{rep}) \ge T(y)]\), the share of replicates whose statistic is at least the observed one. Ties count fully, so a statistic equal to the observed value in every replicate (e.g. absence = 0 throughout) gives \(p = 1\) and flags. The share of ties, \(\Pr[T(y^{rep}) = T(y)]\), is reported as p_tie, so such a flag can be told apart from replicates that all exceed the observed value. The flag is set when p_value is below 0.025 or above 0.975 (Eq. A20). Under a correct model p-values concentrate near 0.5 rather than spreading uniformly, so a flag is a strong signal and an unflagged value is weak evidence of fit.

For a model with an ar() term fitted without cov = TRUE, brms predicts each occasion conditional on the observed lagged residuals, so replicates track the observed series; the autocorrelation check is then conservative and is best read alongside the posterior of the ar coefficient. For non-Gaussian families the ar() term is a latent residual that brms cannot predict for new data, so replicates are drawn on the fitted rows conditional on the fitted latent residuals (and on any observation-level effect), mode = "new" stops with an error, and the returned note says so. Level and immediacy checks are then conservative, while variability and autocorrelation replicates add sampling noise on top of the fitted residuals and can flag without misfit. With a Gaussian ar() term, mode = "new" still conditions each occasion on lagged residuals computed from the observed outcomes and the new-case prediction, so replicates are pulled toward the observed series; the note says so and the generalization check is then conservative.

An observation-level random effect is redrawn, as in the published reference code, which relabels the obs levels and predicts with allow_new_levels = TRUE; conditioning on the fitted effects would make the replicates reproduce the observed values almost exactly, so every check would pass.

Examples

if (interactive()) {
  fit <- run_scd_analysis(simulate_scd_data())$model
  posterior_predictive_features(fit, n_draws = 200)$summary
}
